title: How would you estimate how many laptops UK university students buy each year?
description: A step-by-step estimate for "How many laptops do UK university students buy each year?" with the approach, the maths and a sanity check.
hook: UK university students buy roughly 800,000 laptops a year: about 650,000 bought by new students as they start a course, plus about 160,000 replacements by students already enrolled. Building it from those two moments, starting and replacing, is more accurate than dividing all students by a replacement cycle. Have a go yourself before reading on.
body:
The question

How many laptops do UK university students buy each year?

Three definitions give three different answers, so settle which one you are sizing:

  • Laptops bought by students (or by parents for them) during a year. This is what a retailer cares about, and the default here.
  • The installed base: how many student laptops exist at any time. That is a stock, not a yearly flow.
  • Laptops bought because of university: narrower, excluding a student who upgrades for gaming rather than study.
"I'll estimate new or refurbished laptops bought for students enrolled at UK universities in a year, whoever pays."

The approach: purchases happen at moments

The quick formula is students ÷ years between purchases: 2.9M ÷ 3 = about 967,000. It is a fine first pass, but it assumes every student owns a laptop, replaces it like clockwork and buys only while enrolled. In reality, purchases cluster around two moments:

  1. Starting a course. Many new students buy a laptop for university. Others bring one they already own, or use a work laptop if they study part time.
  2. Replacing during the course. Laptops break, get stolen or become too slow before the course ends.

So the structure is: new entrants × share who buy + continuing students × share who replace.

Step by step

Base figures: HESA counted about 2.9M students at UK higher education providers in 2023/24, of whom about 1.3M were new entrants. That entrant figure is high because it includes postgraduates on one-year courses and part-time students, which is exactly why not every entrant buys a laptop.

GroupStudentsShare buyingLaptops
New entrants1.3M50%650,000
Continuing students (2.9M − 1.3M)1.6M10%160,000
Total2.9M810,000

Why these shares? Half of entrants buying allows for mature, part-time and postgraduate students who already own a suitable machine, and for undergraduates who arrive with a laptop from school. One in ten continuing students replacing a laptop each year matches a machine lasting several years, with accidents on top.

Answer: about 810,000 laptops a year, which is roughly 28 for every 100 students.

Sanity check from a second angle

From the installed base. Assume 90% of the 2.9M students own a laptop: 2.61M machines. If a student laptop lasts about 3.5 years on average, the base turns over at 2.61M ÷ 3.5 = about 750,000 a year. That is within 10% of the bottom-up 810,000, so the two methods agree.

Against the quick formula. The one-line 967,000 sits above both, because it assumes every student is a buyer on a three-year cycle. Explaining why your answer is lower than the shortcut is a sign you have thought about who actually buys.

What it means for a client

About 80% of purchases (650,000 of 810,000) come from new entrants, so demand is heavily seasonal: it peaks between August and October as courses start. A retailer would plan stock, student discounts and marketing around those weeks, and would target parents as well as students, since parents often pay for a first laptop.

What a strong answer sounds like

"I estimate around 800,000 laptops a year. About 650,000 are bought by new students as they start, and 160,000 are replacements. A second method, turning over an installed base of about 2.6 million laptops every three and a half years, gives about 750,000, so I'm comfortable with 750,000 to 800,000. Most of it lands in the autumn term, which matters for anyone selling to students."

A weak answer divides 2.9M by 3, says "about a million" and moves on without asking whether every student is really a buyer.

Common mistakes

  • Treating all entrants as 18-year-old undergraduates. Many entrants are postgraduates, part-time or mature students with different needs.
  • Confusing stock and flow. The number of student laptops in use is not the number bought each year.
  • Double counting. If you add "parents buying for students" as a separate line, you have counted the same laptop twice. Count laptops, not buyers.
  • Ignoring the timing. A yearly total hides the start-of-year peak, which is where a commercial client wins or loses.

Practise it

1. The average student laptop costs $800. How big is the market by value?

Show the answer

810,000 × $800 = $648M a year, or about $650M.

2. A student survey suggests 70% of new entrants buy a laptop, not 50%. What is the new total?

Show the answer

Entrants: 1.3M × 70% = 910,000. Add 160,000 replacements: 1.07M laptops. A 20-point change in one share moves the answer by about a third, which tells you this is the input to check first.

3. A retailer captures 15% of entrant purchases and 5% of replacements. How many laptops does it sell to students?

Show the answer

Entrants: 650,000 × 15% = 97,500. Replacements: 160,000 × 5% = 8,000. Total: 105,500 laptops, about 13% of the market, almost all of it in the start-of-year window.

Where to practise next

For another replacement-cycle estimate, try office chairs bought by UK employers or smartphones sold in India. The full method is in how to answer a market sizing question, and you can practise timed prompts in the market sizing drills.
